<reason>Side B won by directly dismantling Side A's core premises while defending a realistic model of supported home care. Side B effectively showed that Side A's warnings about family burnout and undetected domestic neglect were critiques of an unfunded status quo rather than a system organized around paid home aides and respite care. Furthermore, Side B exposed Side A's economic math as a strawman that assumed every senior requires 24/7 one-on-one staffing, and skillfully trapped Side A into defending premature institutionalization ("early facility placement") for seniors who only need help with daily living today. While Side A argued eloquently about the risks of intermittent supervision and default inertia, it never answered Side B's point that daily visiting professionals spot decline early to guide timely transitions, nor did it refute the institutional harms of overstretched staffing ratios and lethal viral outbreaks.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>In [B3.2], [B4.2]-[B4.3], and [B5.1]-[B5.3], Side B dismantled Side A's argument that progressive cognitive decline requires rejecting a home-care default, forcing Side A to admit in [A4.3] that its model relies on "early facility placement" while elders still have cognitive reserve—which Side B cleanly turned into an indictment of uprooting capable seniors years ahead of schedule.</best_rebuttal>
